In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat al-Falaq

Meccan, and its verses are five.

Imam Muslim narrated from Uqba ibn Amir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Have you not seen that verses have been revealed tonight, the like of which has never been seen: 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak' and 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind'?"

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Uqba ibn Amir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led prayer with these two (surahs) during a journey.

[(p-6305)]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[1–5] ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾: that is, I take refuge in Him and seek His protection. "Al-falaq" is of the form "fa'al" in the sense of "maf'ul" (passive), like "qasas" in the sense of "maqsus" (cut).

Ibn Taymiyya said: Everything that the Lord splits open is a "falaq." Al-Hasan said: "Al-falaq" is everything that splits open from something, such as the dawn, the grain and the date-pit. Al-Zajjaj said: When you reflect on creation, it becomes clear to you that most of it comes from splitting, such as the earth (splitting) with plants and the clouds (splitting) with rain. Many of the exegetes have said: "Al-falaq" is the dawn, for it is said: "This is clearer than the falaq of the dawn and the faraq of the dawn."

Some have said: "Al-falaq" is all of creation. As for those who say it is a valley in Hell, or a tree in Hell, or that it is one of the names of Hell, this is a matter whose soundness we do not know, neither by the indication of the word, nor by transmission from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor is there any wisdom in specifying His lordship in this way. This is unlike saying "Lord of creation," or "Lord of everything that splits open," or "Lord of the light which He makes manifest to His servants by day," for in specifying this by mention there is what displays the greatness of the Lord who is sought refuge in. End.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾: that is, from the evil of what He has created among the two weighty (jinn and humankind) and others, whatever they may be, of beings endowed with natures and choice.

His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿and from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. Abu al-Su'ud said: [(p-6306)] This is the specification of some evils by mention, although they are included in what precedes, because of the greater urgency of the need for seeking refuge and because it calls more strongly to protection.

Imam Ibn Taymiyya said: When it is said that "al-falaq" is both general and specific, then by its generality one seeks refuge from the evil of what He has created, and by its specificity to the daylight one seeks refuge from the evil of the darkness when it settles. The "ghasiq" has been interpreted as the night, as in His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. This is the view of most of the exegetes. The people of language said: The meaning of "waqab" is that it entered into everything. Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-ghasiq" is the cold. The night was called "ghasiq" because it is colder than the day.

Al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Aisha that the Prophet (ﷺ) looked at the moon and said: "O Aisha! Seek refuge in Allah from its evil, for it is the ghasiq when it settles." It was also narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, raised (to the Prophet): "The ghasiq is the star." Ibn Zayd said: It is the Pleiades, and diseases and plagues would increase when it sets and would lift when it rises.

This raised (hadith) has led some people to think that it contradicts those who interpreted it as the night, so they made it a different view, and then interpreted its "waqab" as its stillness. Ibn Qutayba said: It is said: "The ghasiq is the moon when it eclipses and blackens." The meaning of "waqab" is that it entered into the eclipse. This is weak, for what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said cannot be opposed by the saying of another, and he does not say anything except the truth. And he did not command Aisha to seek refuge from it at its eclipse, but rather when it is visible.

Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, and We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day as a seeing one﴾ [al-Isra: 12]. So the moon is the sign of the night, and likewise the stars only rise and are seen at night. Thus His command to seek refuge from that is a command to seek refuge from the sign of the night, its indicator and its mark. The indicator entails what it indicates. So when the evil of the moon exists, the evil of the night exists, and the moon has an influence that nothing else has. Therefore seeking refuge from the evil arising from it is stronger, and this is like His saying concerning the mosque founded on piety: "It is [(p-6307)] my mosque," even though the verse certainly includes the Mosque of Quba. Likewise His saying concerning the People of the Cloak: "These are the People of my House," even though the Qur'an includes his wives. So specification is because the specified is more deserving of the description. Thus the moon is most deserving of seeking refuge (from), and the night is dark, spreading with it the devils of humans and jinn in ways they do not spread by day, and there runs in it kinds of evil that do not run by day: kinds of disbelief, wickedness, disobedience, theft, betrayal, indecencies and other things. So evil is always associated with darkness. For this reason Allah made it for the tranquility and rest of the children of Adam, but the devils of humans and jinn do in it evil that they cannot do by day, and they seek means through the moon, through its invocation and its worship. Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi had a (book called) "Mushaf al-Qamar" (the Book of the Moon), in which he mentions disbelieving and magical matters that suit seeking refuge from it. End of the words of Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then the Exalted specified other created things for seeking refuge from their evil, because of the manifest harm they cause and the difficulty of guarding against them. So it is necessary to resort to Allah and to seek help through His all-encompassing power to repel their evil. He, the Glorified, said: ﴿and from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Ibn Jarir said: That is, from the evil of the sorceresses who blow into the knots of the thread when they perform incantations over it. This is what the people of interpretation said. From Mujahid: it is incantation (ruqya) in the tying of thread. From Tawus: Nothing is closer to shirk than the incantation of the mad. Similar was said by Qatada and al-Hasan. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-naffathat" are the women, or the groups of sorceresses who tie knots in threads, blow upon them and perform incantations. "Al-nafth" is blowing with saliva. There is no effect for that, except if there is the feeding of something harmful, or giving it to drink, or making it smelled, or the touching of the one bewitched by it in some manner. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may do at that time an act as a trial by which those firm upon the truth are distinguished from the literalist (Hashwiyya, a term for uncritical literalists) and the ignorant commoners, and the Hashwiyya and the rabble attribute it to them and to their blowing. But those firm in the firm word do not turn to that nor pay it any heed.

[(p-6308)] If you say: What is the meaning of seeking refuge from their evil? I say: In it are three aspects:

The first: that one seeks refuge from their work, which is the craft of sorcery, and from their sin in that.

The second: that one seeks refuge from their enticing people through their sorcery and what they deceive them with of their falsehood.

The third: that one seeks refuge from what Allah afflicts with evil at their blowing. End.

In the verse there is another interpretation, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him. He said: "Al-naffathat" are the women, and "al-'uqad" (the knots) are the determinations and opinions of men, a metaphor from the knots of ropes. "Al-nafth" is softening the knot of a rope with saliva that one casts upon it, so that its rope becomes easy. So the meaning of the verse is that women, because of the abundance of their love in the hearts of men, manipulate men, turning them from one opinion to another and from one resolve to another. So Allah commanded His Messenger to seek refuge from their evil. Like His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14]. Likewise, Allah magnified their plotting, saying: ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28].

A caution:

Al-Shihab said: It is related in (al-Ta'wilat) from Abu Bakr al-Asamm that he said: The hadith of "his bewitchment, may the blessings of Allah be upon him," which is narrated here, is to be abandoned because of what it entails from the saying of the disbelievers that he was bewitched, and it contradicts the explicit text of the Qur'an, where Allah refuted them. Al-Razi related from al-Qadi that he said: This narration is false, and how is it possible to say it is sound, when Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And Allah protects you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67], and He said: ﴿And the sorcerer does not succeed wherever he comes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]. And because permitting it leads to disparagement of prophethood; and because if it were sound, it would be necessary that they could reach the harm of all the prophets and the righteous, and they would have been able to acquire great dominion for themselves, and all of that is false, and the disbelievers would have been reproaching him by saying he is bewitched. So if this incident had occurred, the disbelievers would have been truthful in that claim, and that defect would have been in him, peace be upon him. And it is known that this is not permissible. End. [(p-6309)] There is no strangeness in this report not being accepted because of what has been proven against it, even if it is recorded in the Sahih collections; for not every report recorded in them is free from criticism, in its chain or its meaning, as the firmly grounded scholars know. Moreover, the scrutiny of solitary reports (khabar al-ahad) is well known from the time of the Companions.

Imam al-Ghazali said in (al-Mustasfa): There is not one of the Companions except that he rejected a solitary report, like the rejection of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, of the report of Abu Sinan al-Ashja'i in the story of (Bar'a bint Wathiq), and it appeared from him that he used to swear an oath regarding the hadith. And like the rejection of Aisha of the report of Ibn Umar regarding "the punishment of the dead for the weeping of their family over them," and it appeared from Umar his prohibiting Abu Musa and Abu Hurayra from narrating hadith from the Messenger (ﷺ), and similar things that have been mentioned. Al-Ghazali included that under the discussions of (the solitary report in knowing the resemblance of those who oppose it). And may Allah have mercy on him, he mentioned in the discussions of (consensus) (ijma') the consensus of the Companions on permitting disagreement with solitary reports, for clear evidences established with them.

Imam Ibn Taymiyya said in (al-Musawwada): The correct view is that whoever rejects a sound report, as the Companions used to reject it, believing the transmitter to be mistaken or lying, because the rejecter believes that the evidence has indicated that the Messenger does not say this, such a person is not to be declared a disbeliever nor a wrongdoer, even if his belief is not correct. For more than one of the Companions rejected more than one report that are sound according to the people of hadith. End.

Al-Allama al-Fanari said in (Fusul al-Bada'i'): The rejecter of solitary reports is not to be called astray, and the matter is well known in the principles (of jurisprudence). I have only expanded in quoting them because I saw among the partisans of the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) one who greatly rejected a report narrated by the likes of al-Bukhari, and declared its denier astray; so I knew that this is ignorance of the discipline of the principles, not of the principles of his own school, as I saw from al-Fanari. Then I said: The custom of the people of opinion is not to give any weight to al-Bukhari, and they have rejected hundreds of his narrations through interpretation and abrogation. So when would they agree with him so as to declare astray one who rejects a report in it? And he (al-Fanari) proved his claim and stood defending the Messenger of Allah and his chosen one.

Furthermore, the discussion of this hadith is famous, old and new, and the commentators of (al-Sahih) and Ibn Qutayba in his commentary (Ta'wil Mukhtalif al-Hadith) and al-Razi have extensively spoken about it. The truth is not hidden from its seeker. And Allah knows best.

﴿and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, when he displays his envy and acts upon what it requires of seeking the calamities of the envied. For if the effect of what he conceals does not appear, no harm returns from it to the envied, but rather it is harmful to himself, because of his distress at the joy of others.

The third: that one seeks refuge from what Allah afflicts with evil at their blowing. End.

Thus His command to seek refuge from that is a command to seek refuge from the sign of the night, its indicator and its mark. The indicator entails what it indicates. So when the evil of the moon exists, the evil of the night exists, and the moon has an influence that nothing else has. Therefore seeking refuge from the evil arising from it is stronger, and this is like His saying concerning the mosque founded on piety: "It is [(p-6307)] my mosque," even though the verse certainly includes the Mosque of Quba. Likewise His saying concerning the People of the Cloak: "These are the People of my House," even though the Qur'an includes his wives. So specification is because the specified is more deserving of the description. Thus the moon is most deserving of seeking refuge (from), and the night is dark, spreading with it the devils of humans and jinn in ways they do not spread by day, and there runs in it kinds of evil that do not run by day: kinds of disbelief, wickedness, disobedience, theft, betrayal, indecencies and other things. So evil is always associated with darkness. For this reason Allah made it for the tranquility and rest of the children of Adam, but the devils of humans and jinn do in it evil that they cannot do by day, and they seek means through the moon, through its invocation and its worship. Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi had a (book called) "Mushaf al-Qamar" (the Book of the Moon), in which he mentions disbelieving and magical matters that suit seeking refuge from it. End of the words of Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then the Exalted specified other created things for seeking refuge from their evil, because of the manifest harm they cause and the difficulty of guarding against them. So it is necessary to resort to Allah and to seek help through His all-encompassing power to repel their evil. He, the Glorified, said: ﴿and from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Ibn Jarir said: That is, from the evil of the sorceresses who blow into the knots of the thread when they perform incantations over it. This is what the people of interpretation said. From Mujahid: it is incantation (ruqya) in the tying of thread. From Tawus: Nothing is closer to shirk than the incantation of the mad. Similar was said by Qatada and al-Hasan. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-naffathat" are the women, or the groups of sorceresses who tie knots in threads, blow upon them and perform incantations. "Al-nafth" is blowing with saliva. There is no effect for that, except if there is the feeding of something harmful, or giving it to drink, or making it smelled, or the touching of the one bewitched by it in some manner. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may do at that time an act as a trial by which those firm upon the truth are distinguished from the literalist (Hashwiyya, a term for uncritical literalists) and the ignorant commoners, and the Hashwiyya and the rabble attribute it to them and to their blowing. But those firm in the firm word do not turn to that nor pay it any heed.

[(p-6308)] If you say: What is the meaning of seeking refuge from their evil? I say: In it are three aspects:

The first: that one seeks refuge from their work, which is the craft of sorcery, and from their sin in that.

The second: that one seeks refuge from their enticing people through their sorcery and what they deceive them with of their falsehood.

The third: that one seeks refuge from what Allah afflicts with evil at their blowing. End.

In the verse there is another interpretation, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him. He said: "Al-naffathat" are the women, and "al-'uqad" (the knots) are the determinations and opinions of men, a metaphor from the knots of ropes. "Al-nafth" is softening the knot of a rope with saliva that one casts upon it, so that its rope becomes easy. So the meaning of the verse is that women, because of the abundance of their love in the hearts of men, manipulate men, turning them from one opinion to another and from one resolve to another. So Allah commanded His Messenger to seek refuge from their evil. Like His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14]. Likewise, Allah magnified their plotting, saying: ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28].

A caution:

Al-Shihab said: It is related in (al-Ta'wilat) from Abu Bakr al-Asamm that he said: The hadith of "his bewitchment, may the blessings of Allah be upon him," which is narrated here, is to be abandoned because of what it entails from the saying of the disbelievers that he was bewitched, and it contradicts the explicit text of the Qur'an, where Allah refuted them. Al-Razi related from al-Qadi that he said: This narration is false, and how is it possible to say it is sound, when Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And Allah protects you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67], and He said: ﴿And the sorcerer does not succeed wherever he comes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]. And because permitting it leads to disparagement of prophethood; and because if it were sound, it would be necessary that they could reach the harm of all the prophets and the righteous, and they would have been able to acquire great dominion for themselves, and all of that is false, and the disbelievers would have been reproaching him by saying he is bewitched. So if this incident had occurred, the disbelievers would have been truthful in that claim, and that defect would have been in him, peace be upon him. And it is known that this is not permissible. End. [(p-6309)] There is no strangeness in this report not being accepted because of what has been proven against it, even if it is recorded in the Sahih collections; for not every report recorded in them is free from criticism, in its chain or its meaning, as the firmly grounded scholars know. Moreover, the scrutiny of solitary reports (khabar al-ahad) is well known from the time of the Companions.

Imam al-Ghazali said in (al-Mustasfa): There is not one of the Companions except that he rejected a solitary report, like the rejection of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, of the report of Abu Sinan al-Ashja'i in the story of (Bar'a bint Wathiq), and it appeared from him that he used to swear an oath regarding the hadith. And like the rejection of Aisha of the report of Ibn Umar regarding "the punishment of the dead for the weeping of their family over them," and it appeared from Umar his prohibiting Abu Musa and Abu Hurayra from narrating hadith from the Messenger (ﷺ), and similar things that have been mentioned. Al-Ghazali included that under the discussions of (the solitary report in knowing the resemblance of those who oppose it). And may Allah have mercy on him, he mentioned in the discussions of (consensus) (ijma') the consensus of the Companions on permitting disagreement with solitary reports, for clear evidences established with them.

Imam Ibn Taymiyya said in (al-Musawwada): The correct view is that whoever rejects a sound report, as the Companions used to reject it, believing the transmitter to be mistaken or lying, because the rejecter believes that the evidence has indicated that the Messenger does not say this, such a person is not to be declared a disbeliever nor a wrongdoer, even if his belief is not correct. For more than one of the Companions rejected more than one report that are sound according to the people of hadith. End.

Al-Allama al-Fanari said in (Fusul al-Bada'i'): The rejecter of solitary reports is not to be called astray, and the matter is well known in the principles (of jurisprudence). I have only expanded in quoting them because I saw among the partisans of the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) one who greatly rejected a report narrated by the likes of al-Bukhari, and declared its denier astray; so I knew that this is ignorance of the discipline of the principles, not of the principles of his own school, as I saw from al-Fanari. Then I said: The custom of the people of opinion is not to give any weight to al-Bukhari, and they have rejected hundreds of his narrations through interpretation and abrogation. So when would they agree with him so as to declare astray one who rejects a report in it? And he (al-Fanari) proved his claim and stood defending the Messenger of Allah and his chosen one.

Furthermore, the discussion of this hadith is famous, old and new, and the commentators of (al-Sahih) and Ibn Qutayba in his commentary (Ta'wil Mukhtalif al-Hadith) and al-Razi have extensively spoken about it. The truth is not hidden from its seeker. And Allah knows best.

﴿and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, when he displays his envy and acts upon what it requires of seeking the calamities of the envied. For if the effect of what he conceals does not appear, no harm returns from it to the envied, but rather it is harmful to himself, because of his distress at the joy of others.
